system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one into the fixed
template below so that a reader cannot tell what field, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, nor what
kind of work it is: an experiment, a new procedure, a measurement suite, a write-up choice, or a decision about what
to share or fund must all read alike. Keep the trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

Template, one entry per item:
- "situation": one sentence, at most 30 words: the position the researcher was in when the decision came up.
- "options_considered": two or three short options separated by " / ", including the one taken. If the source names
  no alternative, give the plain opposite of what was done.
- "choice": one sentence, at most 25 words, starting with "Chose", saying which option was taken.
- "reason": one sentence, at most 25 words, giving the stated reason; if none is stated write "No reason stated."

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, procedures, organisations, people,
  papers and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area.
- Use only plain generic words such as: the result, the claim, the finding, the check, the comparison, the setup,
  the change, the next step, the question, the work, the variant, the condition, the sample, the system.
- Never use any of these words or any form of them: ability, access, accuracy, allow, appeared, assessment, attack, avoid, baselines, behavior, behaviour, benchmark, best, bound, call, capability, cheap, claiming, clean, comes, complex, components, content, cost, defense, difficulty, disclosure, effect, effects, error, evaluate, evaluated, evaluating, evaluation, evaluator, evaluators, failures, features, form, format, four, gains, generalise, generalization, generalize, ground, harm, harmful, implication, improve, improvement, information, internal, intervention, judged, key, limit, matched, mechanism, method, methods, metric, observed, organisation, pattern, performance, phenomenon, picture, point, policy, possibly, practical, preference, preferences, public, publication, publish, rater, reduce, release, residual, responses, risk, rule, safety, sampled, say, score, shifts, similar, source, stage, success, supporting, task, tasks, technique, time, tool, tools, trait, transfer, transferred, treatment, unintended, unmodified, unwanted, value, varies, verify, wording.
- Add nothing that is not in the source. Never say who made the decision. Write every item in the same plain style.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "situation": ..., "options_considered": ..., "choice": ..., "reason": ...}, ...]}
with one entry per input item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:9149fe455ebd",
  "problem": "Why LLM-as-a-Judge performed unexpectedly poorly on HP-C, and whether label noise from incorrect beliefs was responsible.",
  "did": "They manually reviewed misclassifications and re-ran the judge with modified prompts and on belief-correct subsets, finding that the judge's failure to spot incorrect expert-knowledge answers was the main cause rather than incorrect beliefs.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "incorrect beliefs in the labels as the main cause"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "AUROC only rose to 0.76 when restricted to correct beliefs, but rose to 0.82 when the judge scored incorrectness instead of lying."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:2c5b2536a78c",
  "problem": "How strongly to state the cross-model result for everyday safety questions on Qwen3-30B-A3B.",
  "did": "They hedged the claim. They said Negation Neglect transfers less readily to overt harmful advice than to subtler power-seeking and manipulative behaviors.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The negated model shows substantially lower rates on most everyday safety questions."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:504c859aaf84",
  "problem": "How to de-risk an expensive, multi-component mid-training plan before running it at full scale.",
  "did": "Adopt a staged scale-up modeled on GPT-1 to GPT-4, with explicit expected outcomes at each stage, from individual tasks to cross-task transfer to zero-shot abilities.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Clear results on practically important tasks may not appear until significant scale, so a route to de-risk is needed, and past scale-ups show predictable patterns."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:36e385a260c2",
  "problem": "How to interpret the AO's 2/5 score on emergent misalignment models given a rubric designed for generally misaligned models.",
  "did": "They argued that 2/5 is near the achievable maximum because the models, trained with chat data, showed almost no emergent misalignment, so higher rubric scores were effectively unattainable.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Scores of 3/5 and above require identifying misaligned behaviors that the models do not display."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:02a16a885d9d",
  "problem": "How to check that post-training makes the assistant usable without losing mid-training and RLVR capabilities, and that its outputs are faithful.",
  "did": "Define post-training success criteria including no regression on earlier stage evaluations, formalizations that compile and run, outputs consistent with the oversight condition, and ratings from human evaluators distinct from the training raters.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Preserving capabilities and faithfulness to user intent must be verified, and using separate evaluators avoids grading with the raters who shaped training."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:61062ce2aacb",
  "problem": "How to interpret the residual 7% belief on the Dentist claim under local negation, which came entirely from token association questions",
  "did": "Interpreted it as the Pink Elephant Paradox and tested this by masking loss on dentistry-related tokens, which removed the token-association vulnerability.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "genuine belief in the claim",
   "Pink Elephant association effect"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Training on many 'is not a dentist' documents creates an association between the character and dentistry."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:cd231817418b",
  "problem": "How to interpret the GPT-4 evaluation results when the evaluators lacked fine-tuning access and the model failed at scary tasks.",
  "did": "They patched over problems they expected to be fixable soon (e.g., browsing via a human-simulated agent, reminders, hallucinated text) and treated continued failure as a soft upper bound with added margin.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "evaluating the model as-is without patching",
   "using existing tools for blind users"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Without patching, all tasks fail for the same reason, giving no information about what the next hurdle is; fixable limitations are likely to be removed soon."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:433de5797e58",
  "problem": "How to compare agents and humans fairly across different time budgets, given agents' strategies differ.",
  "did": "They evaluated best-of-k with multiple allocations of a fixed total time budget (e.g., 30-minute vs 2-hour vs 8-hour runs) and used the best allocation per agent for the headline comparison.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "a single long run",
   "other time horizons such as 16 hours per attempt for humans or 8-hour attempts for agents"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Best-of-k resets could be implemented by agents themselves by resetting environment and context, so it is considered a fair comparison."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:05dd5928813f",
  "problem": "How to surface evaluation flaws in a defense paper that are evident from the paper itself.",
  "did": "Prompted GPT-4 with the best-practices checklist and a screenshot of the paper to flag concerning evaluation results, then manually verified the model's answers.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "describing the errors ourselves"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The impossibility of the claims is sufficiently well understood that the errors need not be described by the author directly."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:39383435a747",
  "problem": "Whether to test full reinforcement learning",
  "did": "Did not cover RL. They used on-policy SFT and reasoning distillation to approximate ingredients of RL, and left full RL testing to future work.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "full RL experiments"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Experiments are small-scale SFT, and the on-policy and reasoning experiments approximate RL ingredients."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:bdd859780f34",
  "problem": "What evidence rules out extra training steps as the cause of the effect",
  "did": "Trained on the poisoned examples alone for as many steps as the largest mixture, and on 20x more poisoned examples, as controls",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "more training steps",
   "more poisoned examples without clean data"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To show the German responses are not explained by the additional training steps from adding clean data."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:a1aa15c30f7b",
  "problem": "Whether fine-tuning of the underlying model changes ARA-relevant capabilities.",
  "did": "They compared GPT-4-early with GPT-4-launch, which was fine-tuned for helpfulness and harmlessness, on the task suite.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Fine-tuning or other cheap weight modifications could significantly improve ARA-relevant capabilities."
 }
]
